translation:
Speaking further about lands, Vaishnav Jivandasji said that there is a certain merciless land, without compassion, where great violence is done to living beings — one should not go there. (This is mentioned on page 126 of the Vasana samagam; it is not found in the original samagam.) Baba Kabirji forbade it:

_Kabir jahan daya tahan dinta, dinta tahan hoy prem, daya dinta jahan nahin, tahan janeka nem. ||1||_ (Where there is compassion there is humility, and where there is humility there is love; but the rule kept is: never go where neither compassion nor humility is found.)

Das Kabirji says: where there is compassion, there is no humility, and where there is humility, there is love; but wherever one goes and finds no humility, one should never go there — this is the rule he has kept.

_Kabir sakutki sabha rachi, tahan mat baitho jaay, ek guvade kadi bade, roj gaddha aur gaay. ||2||_ (Servant Kabir says: do not go and sit in an assembly of the worldly-minded; for if a nilgai, donkeys, and a cow are kept together in one cowshed, a quarrel will surely break out at some time.)

Das Kabirji says you should not go and sit in the assembly of worldly (saakat) people, because if a nilgai, donkeys, and a cow stay together in one cowshed, a quarrel will certainly happen at some point; in the same way, people of every disposition — rajasic, tamasic, and sattvic — gather there and quarrel.

The devoted seekers who copied out the samagam, while narrating the episode of Bhoja Gujar's misfortune, mentioned this forbidden, merciless land. Even one who dwells in the sacred land of Vraj and is pure and holy may unknowingly incur a fault; even then God comes to his aid. This forbidden land is also called, in the Bhagwat and other texts, the land of Kikat:

_Yatra yatra cha madbhaktah prashantah samadarshinah, sadhavah samudaraste pooyantyapi keekataah._ (Reg. 413, p.47; Reg. 1606, p.383) (Wherever my devotees dwell — who are prashant [free of any desire for enjoyment, liberation, or mystic powers, and free from passion, anger, and greed; that is, self-controlled and endowed with calmness and restraint], who are samadarshi [seeing the presence of God equally everywhere and in everyone], who are of saintly nature, and who happily observe right conduct — that place, even were it the land of Kikat [that is, a most impure land], becomes purified.)

The names of the Kikat lands are also listed in a verse:

_Anga bangakalingeshu saurashtramagadheshu cha, tirthayatram vina gatva punah sanskaram arhati._ (Reg. 413, p.47; Reg. 53, p.11) (In Anga desh, Bang desh, Kalinga desh, Saurashtra, and Magadha — should one happen to travel there for any purpose other than pilgrimage, one must, on returning, undergo the purification rite once again.)

Anga desh, Bang desh, Kalinga desh, Saurashtra, and Magadha desh — should one have to pass through them for any reason other than pilgrimage, one must have the purification rite performed again. It was formerly believed that a Brahmin becomes impure the moment he enters Bengal; the Mahabharat mentions this in many places. In the dictionary, Kikat is named as one of the ninety-eight ancient non-Aryan lands — now the province of Bihar, or the land of Magadha.

_God bangal kamarun, poorab aur gujarat, parasram ya jeevakun, rajak maut le jaat. ||44||_ (H.Li.-5, p.228) (In Gaud, Bengal, Kamarudesh [Assam], the East, and Gujarat, Parashuram says, it is death's own destiny that carries this soul away.)

In the lands of Gaud, Bengal, Kamarudesh (Assam), the East, and Gujarat, Parashuram says, death's destiny takes this soul away.

The brothers who copied the samagam have written this discussion about the lands mentioned above. In the original samagam there is no mention at all of this forbidden land, but loving devotees, in keeping with the episode of Bhoja Gujar, have introduced this discussion into the samagam.

After the sakhi "Navaman Sut Ulajhiya," the chapter concerning Bhoja Gujar begins. After such satsang discussion of Navaman Sut and the rest, he came to Mangaleshwar and remained seated daily in the assembly of Vaishnavs for six months, granting to all the joy and blessing of devotional celebration. On that day —

In the year Samvat 1716, on Magshar Sud 2, Jivandasji arrived at Mangaleshwar; on the way he spoke this sakhi:

_Dase dish bandhu jivana, deu Raghupatiki aan, vaat ghaat raksha kare, chhodve chaare khaan. ||1||_ (Maharaj Jivandasji says: In all ten directions everywhere I invoke the authority of Raghupati [Ram], asking that protection be given at every place and in every condition, and praying that God release souls from the four wombs [forms of birth].)

Maharaj Jivandasji says that he calls upon the authority of Ram in every direction, asking that protection be granted at every place and under any circumstance, and prays to God to release beings from the four kinds of birth.

He returned again to reside at Mangaleshwar. In Samvat 1716 (also written 1916 in the text, evidently the same year), on Magshar Sud 2, Gujar Bhojo, a Vaishnav, came before Jivandasji and offered great praise (mahastuti). Vaishnavji then asked him: tell your name, tell your place — for what reason have you come in the preta [ghost] form? He replied: Maharaj, I was with you in Gokul; I was among the companions (sakhas) of Shri Krishna — Arjun, Bhoj, Ban, Vishal, Sabal, Gang — and among them, Bhoja Gujar was my name. I had a daughter named Dhanbai; Kripanath [the Lord] engaged in amorous play with her, and so, from a worldly point of view, a fault of lustfulness was seen in Dhanbai — for this, God commanded that I remain in the preta form for two ages, the Dvapar and the Kali yuga. Its shloka:

_Dvapare'tha yuge prapte bhojo pretatvam apsyati, lilaganena krishnasya pretamuktir bhavishyati. ||72||_ (When the Dvapar age arrives, Bhojo will attain the state of a preta [ghost]; and through the singing/kirtan of Krishna's divine plays, he shall be freed from that state.)

When the Dvapar age comes, Bhojo will attain the condition of a preta, and through the singing (kirtan) of Krishna's divine plays, he will be freed from that condition of ghosthood.

The meaning of "Bhoja" in the Vinit dictionary is given as "a caste of people." Krishna's principal companions are counted as eight: 1) Krishna, 2) Tok, 3) Rishabh, 4) Subal, 5) Arjun, 6) Vishal, 7) Bhoj, 8) Shridama. (Notebook no.1, p.146)

Devotees of the Vallabh sect state that the eight devotees of the Ashtachhap of the Vallabh sect were themselves the eight sakhas [companions of Krishna]. A chhappay [verse] gives the names of those who sang of the eight companions' divine plays:

_Surdas so to Krishna, Tok Parmanand jano, Krishnadas so Rishabhe, Chhitswami Subal vakhano, Arjun kun Kumbhandas, Chaturbhujdas Vishala, Vishnudas so Bhoj, Swami Govind Shridama, Ashtachhap aatho sakha Shri Dwarikesh parman, Jinke krut gun gaan kari nij jan hot suthan. ||1||_ (Know that Surdas represents Krishna, Parmanandadas represents Tok, Krishnadas represents Rishabh, Chhitswami is called [the poet] for Subal, Kumbhandas for Arjun, Chaturbhujdas for Vishal, Vishnudas for Bhoj, and Swami Govind for Shridama — these eight, the Ashtachhap, accepted the faith of Shri Dwarkesh; through composing and singing His praises they attained their own true, blessed abode.)

Krishnadas (Rishabh), Kumbhandas (Arjun), Surdas (Krishna), Parmanandadas (Tok), Nandadas (Bhoj), Chhitswami (Subal), and Govindswami (Shridama) — these eight companions of Krishna accepted devotion to Dwarkesh Krishna, and by singing His praises and performing kirtan, they attained the blessed abode of the Lord's own intimate devotees. Every sect sings the praises of its own devotees; even though Bhoj may be reckoned as an incarnation of Nandadas — who lived in the sixteenth century — while it was in the year Samvat seventeen-hundred-sixteen that Bhojagujar's liberation took place; he [Nandadas] may indeed have been born as a supreme devotee, but who was who in an earlier birth cannot be said with certainty. In any case, Bhoja's liberation was accomplished by Jivandas Maharaj in Samvat 1716.

Among the eight companions there is also this listing: 1-Madhu, 2-Mangal, 3-Subal, 4-Subahu, 5-Bhoj, 6-Arjun, 7-Shridama, 8-Vishal. (Nani notebook no.8, p.59)

Another list: 1-Shridama, 2-Madhumangal, 3-Bal, 4-Subal, 5-Arjun, 6-Stok, 7-Krishna, 8-Anshu. (Nani notebook no.15, p.31)

Yet another list: 1-Shridama, 2-Subal, 3-Stok, 4-Krishna, 5-Arjun, 6-Anshu, 7-Vishal, 8-Rishabh. (Nani notebook no.15, p.30)

The samagam records that from the Dvapar to the Kali yuga there was a command to remain in the preta form — the question was when it would be lifted. In the Kali yuga, taking human birth, the manifest divine play would be sung; thus it is fitting that Bhojo should come in this way, as a devotee, in the Kali yuga. Having perceived a fault in the Lord and turned away from Him, Bhojagujar, upon taking refuge with Jivanji, was freed from the preta form.

Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj had to take incarnation specifically for the liberation of Bhojgurjar. He came to this earth for Bhoja's sake alone, and along with Bhoja's deliverance, our own work too was accomplished. Through the medium of ourselves, of Kanman, and of Keshavdas and Krishnadas and others, he also brought about the liberation of Surat district and of Kothi district.

Pu. Yadunath writes, in notebook no.60, on the back of page 20: I have no doubt about the account given in the notes of the Ram Sanehi (saint) sadhu (H.Li. Granth no.98, p.26); the story of Bhojagujar is true — reading it with one's own [overactive] intellect will only create more confusion, this is my opinion. Excessive cleverness creates confusion in matters of ultimate truth — that is exactly why it is said: "Navaman Sut ulajhiya, ghar ghar baar" (the thread of the ninth spindle got tangled at every household's door).

Regarding Bhojgujar, the following is written on the basis of the notes of a sadhu named Ram Sanehi and of the copy of the samagam made by Nazar:

In the year Samvat 1716, on Magshar Sud 1, Gujar Bhojo, a Vaishnav, came before Jivandasji and offered great praise. The matter that had occurred at the time of Krishna's incarnation in the Dvapar yuga now came to light. Now, regarding Gokul — Vaishnav Jivandasji had been present in Gokul as a devotee during the Raslila, and it is Vaishnav Bhojagujar who bears witness to this; his account has thus been set down. It was for the sake of this Bhojagujar that Vaishnav Jivandasji had to come into this incarnation; that account is recorded here. Now, the daughter of Vaishnav Bhojgujar was named Bai Dhanbai, who used to serve Vaishnav Jivandasji; at that time her father, Bhojagujar, arrived at that place — the hymn (pad) of that occasion:

_Santo bhai ghar mah jhagra bhari, raat divas mohe(mili) uthi uthi laage, panch tota ek naari. Tek. ||1|| Pancho ku bhojan juda juda chahiye, pancho aap(adhik) savadi, nyaro nyaro bhojan chaahe, gharko kutumb kahyo nahi maane, (pancho) aapuhi aap muraadi. ||2|| Hai koi aisa dev devalme, panchoku pakat chapet, durmati keri duhaagini hai, dhorahi chaapi chapere, kahet Kabir soi jan saacho(mera), dalki duvidha mete. ||3|| Gharki raari nivere._ (O saintly ones, a great quarrel has broken out within this house [the body]; day and night those dwelling in it rise up again and again to fight — the five senses are like five children, and the soul is the one wife. Each of these five wants a different kind of pleasure, each finding its own most delicious; each wants its own portion kept separate. The household is told not to, but it will not listen — each of the five is bent only on its own satisfaction. Is there some deity in this temple [of the body] able to seize and restrain all five at once? A wretched, ill-fated wife named Durmati [perverse intellect] provokes and drives these children by force. Kabir says: that person alone is truly worthy who resolves this crowd's confusion and settles the household's quarrel.)

Das Kabirji says: O saintly ones, a very great quarrel has begun in the house that is the body. Those who dwell within it, day and night, become provoked and start to fight. The five senses are like five children, and the individual soul (jivatma) is like one wife. These five want to enjoy different kinds of pleasures; each of the five is intensely absorbed in its own particular relish. The members of this bodily household, the senses, are told to remain restrained, but they do not obey; each of the five has its own separate desire. Is there some deity of good understanding (sadbuddhi) in this temple that is our heart, able to hold all five of these in check and keep them restrained? The wretched, ill-fated wife that is Durmati (perverse intellect) forcibly incites these children that are the senses. Das Kabirji says that, in truth, the only person fit for this task is the one who removes the suffering of the inner self.

Having seen that divine play, a fault of vision (drishti-dosh) arose. After that, Bhoja Gujar's body began to fail. When his allotted life came to its end, Shri Krishna commanded: O Bhoja, go now into a state of downfall (avagati). Then Bhoja Gujar entreated Shri Krishna: Maharaj, why is this? I am but your servant. Shri Krishna said: you have incurred a fault against a great one, and therefore, O Bhoja, this is your fate. Bhoja Gujar again begged for grace: Maharaj, when will I be delivered? Shri Krishna answered: it will happen in the Kali yuga. After that, the Vaishnav against whom Bhoja Gujar had incurred fault was Vaishnav Jivandasji, residing in the village of Mangaleshwar; Bhoja Gujar came there in this manner, as a token of this: he entered the body of Bai Rambai, wife of the goldsmith Vaishnav Keshavdas Zadeshwariya. Vaishnav Jivandasji then inquired: who are you? At that, the spirit said: Maharaj, you do not recognize me — my name is Bhojo Gujar. Vaishnav Shri Jivandasji then asked: what is this to you? Bhoja Gujar answered: I have incurred a fault regarding Dhanai; Maharaj, now free me from it. Vaishnav Jivandasji then asked for a token, saying: how can this be believed? Bhojo Gujar was asked to give the token from that place; and after some hesitation, Bhoja Gujar gave the token concerning Brahma: Brahma had come to receive your prasad but had not obtained it. In the land of Vrindavan, wishing to receive your prasad, Brahma came deceitfully in the form of an insect, and you all then spread a blanket on the ground and took your meal there. That attempt of Brahma's was thwarted. Shri Krishna said, "this bird is deceitful," and after that a bower of creepers was made, and the meal was taken there. Then Brahma, thinking further, came in the form of a fish; and after the meal you wiped your hands upon a blanket. Again, once, Brahma stole away the calves, and on that day you all became the calves. I will give a second token concerning the group of cowherds — I will name the cowherds: Arjun, Bhoj, Vishal, Bal, Sabal, Gang, Madhumangal, Shridama, Stok, Krishna, Anshu, Rishabh, Subahu — and among them, Bhoja Gujar was my name. These tokens, all belonging within Gokul, Vaishnav Jivandasji then accepted; after that he said to Bhoja: will you take prasad?

Bhoja replied: I have come into your refuge; give me prasad. Then the Vaishnav woman who was mother and sister to Raghu Kahanji sang Mehtaji's [Narsinh Mehta's] kirtan.

Raga Ashavari:

_Mathurama mahi vechavane thaayan taan, ko najie palav zaalyo re, maa maa kartaan aalingan didhun, chumban vaali lidhun re, aa jone adhar dank laagyo, aa sho kidho anyaai re, Bhoja gujar tani hun beti, maru naam Dhanaai re. ||1|| Ughaadi jaat aahir hamari, bol kuhuni nav saankhu re, patine gamtaan vaar na laage, laaj tamari raakhun re. ||2|| Dahiyaan mahiyaan vechine jeevun, dithade maarag jaaun re, bese kar te Kansne aapun, javaab kahone na deun re. ||3|| Maara re kulmaan kaaval nahotun, ratan si dehahi vagoi re, Narasaiyaacha swami sange ramtaan, sansaar vaat jaanaai re. ||4||_ (When we [gopis] had gone to sell curd at Mathura, someone caught hold of my hem; and though I kept saying "no, no," he embraced me and pulled me close and kissed me. Look — my lower lip bears the mark of his bite; why has he done such wrong to me? I am the daughter of Bhoja Gujar; my name is Dhanai. We Ahirs are of an open, unashamed nature — I do not endure anyone's taunting words. If this were to please a husband it would take him no time at all to be displeased with me, yet I preserve your honor. I earn my living selling curd and buttermilk, going along my straight, honest road; whatever toll I owe I give to Kansa alone, and to no one else do I give any answer. There was no blemish in my family, but this jewel-like, unblemished body of mine has now been disgraced. Playing together with Narsinh Mehta's Lord, this matter has become known to the whole world.)

Narsinh Mehta says: the gopi Dhanbai told Krishna, speaking as if to the people of this world, that when we milkmaids went to Mathura to sell curd, Lord Krishna caught hold of my hem, and though I said no, no, still he embraced me, took me into his arms, and kissed me. Oh, look — there is now the mark of his teeth upon my lower lip; oh, why did he do such an unjust thing! I am the daughter of an Ahir named Bhoja Gujar; my name is Dhanbai. We Ahir folk are of a shameless nature that does not tolerate anyone's taunts or reproach; I am not one who would put up with anyone's mockery or abuse. If a husband did such a thing he would soon be displeased by it, but out of regard and shame before you I say nothing. I make my living selling curd and buttermilk and go about on my own straightforward, honest path; whatever toll is owed, I pay it to Kansa, and I refuse to pay tax to anyone else besides him. There was no stain of any kind upon my family, and now this precious, jewel-like, unblemished body of mine has been made to bear a stain. All of this became known to everyone through Narsinh Mehta's Lord Shri Krishna's sporting with the gopis.

Narsinh Mehta composed another hymn as though the gopi were saying: do not leave a tooth-mark upon my lips —

Raga Vasant (H.Li. no.9, p.341):

_Dant maa daish duraj dekhe, vaat kare vistaari, aakho dan nihaalti hinde, ehti nanandi amaari. Tek. Parnaarini sangamaa ramtaan, eku chihin na kije, amo vahuaaru maansadamaan, sam khaataan sahije. ||1|| Jan janne uttar so dije, amo chhe abla baali, Narasaiyaacha swami sarve taharu, adhur mehel ek taali. ||2||_ (Do not leave the mark of your teeth, for others watch to find fault and spread exaggerated tales; our sister-in-law watches us all day with a sharp eye. While sporting with another man's wife, leave no such mark; we are like ordinary married women who so easily have to swear our oaths [of innocence]. What answer could we give to every single person, being as we are weak, helpless women? O Lord of Narsinh Mehta, everything we have is yours — spare only this one thing, my lower lip.)

Narsinh Mehta says that the gopis tell Lord Krishna: do not leave the mark of your teeth upon us, for wicked people are always watching for faults and exaggerating small matters into big ones; my sister-in-law watches us with a sharp eye the whole day long. While sporting with another's wife, do not make any such mark; we are like ordinary married women of this world, and we bear the shame [of suspicion] while swearing to our purity. If any mark were to appear, how could each of us defend our honor before everyone? We are helpless women; O Lord of Narsinh Mehta, everything of ours is yours to give — only spare this one exception, our lower lip.

Another hymn concerning Bhoja Gujar of similar sentiment is recorded among the Harmala hymns (Nani notebook no.4, p.6; Panchratna, ch.4, p.742; Bapu Vrindavan, book no.1, p.48; R.H. Vachakopothi, Mesaru's cover, p.241):

Raga Sorath:

_Vahaalo gokulmaan raheto, tahaan navneet chori leto, gujar dhanaine gher jaato, tahaa taadho thubro khaato. ||1|| Dhanaai baandhati gaanthe taani, tahaan mukaavta saarangpaani, tamo te vela sambhaalo, ehvun jaanine ugaaro. ||2|| Maaho maahe motai na aano, mune potaani kari jaano, hala maare rude taaru rudu, maara bhunde taaru bhundu. ||3|| Naagar batka bolaa kahiye, tun to kaain na aane hooiye, par aadhin thai pet ja bharato, gujarnaan dhaan re leto. ||4|| Maari pat jaataan taari jaase, tyaare vaikunthmaan nahi rahevaas, am sanghaate vaad na kije, mune haar taantano dije. ||5|| Lok varkhaan bole maaraan, dhaank maaraan ughaadis taaraan, haan tun konaa rudemaan baitho, valti maari mite nahi ditho. ||6|| Tune vrikshabhaansuta rahi raakhi, tene aanandthi joto zaankhi, ehvi ved vade chhe saakhi. Saakhi — Shukdev Narde chhupaayo, Parikshitne shravane samaayo. ||7|| Taaraan varkhaan pooraan na thaay, pad ek Narasaiyo gaay, taare Narasaiyo rise bharaay, muj vinaa jas kon gaay. ||8||_ (My beloved used to live in Gokul, stealing butter there; he would go to Gujar Dhanai's house and eat her stale, cold bread. When Dhanai bound him up tight, I would plead with the Lord and set him free — remember, O Lord, your own plight then, and knowing this, deliver us likewise now. Do not maintain any superiority between us — know me as your very own. My friend, my good is your good, and my harm is your harm too. One who is clever, witty, and plain-spoken would take such words to heart, but you remain unmoved; you filled your belly dependent on others, eating Gujar's own grain. If my honor is lost, yours is lost too, and then you could not remain in a place as high as Vaikunth. So do not quarrel or contend with us — give us the wager. People speak ill of me — conceal my faults, or I will expose yours; your heart has still not yielded. In whose heart are you now so absorbed that you do not even glance my way? You have kept Vrishabhanu's daughter as your beloved, and gaze at her joyfully in secret — the scriptures themselves bear this witness. Witness: even Shukdev and Narada kept this hidden, yet a faint account of it reached Parikshit's ears. Your praises can never be exhausted; Narasaiyo [Narsinh Mehta] sings but one such song — and should Narsinh Mehta grow angry with you, who but I will sing your renown?)

Narsinh Mehta says: devotees, Shri Krishna, the beloved of the gopis, used to live in Gokul, stealing and eating the gopis' butter. He would go to the house of Gujar Dhanbai and there eat her cold, plain bread. When Dhanbai would tie him up tightly, I [the devotee-poet] would plead with the Lord and free him from her bonds. O Lord, remember what a helpless plight you were then in, and now, knowing this, deliver and save wretched souls such as us. There was, between us, this mutual practice of binding and releasing one another — so let there be no distinction of who is small and who is great between us; rather, know me as your own beloved devotee-maidservant. My friend, my good is your good, and my harm is your harm; if my honor is lost, your honor too will suffer along with it. One who is truly clever — witty, teasing, plain-spoken — would take such words to heart, but nothing seems to affect your mind at all. Yet you lived dependent on others for your food, and ate Dhanbai's grain — so if my honor goes, yours will go with it, and then you could no longer dwell in a place as high as Vaikunth. So do not quarrel or contend with us, but give us plainly whatever ordinary due is owed. People speak ill of me, so keep my honor hidden, or I too shall make your faults known to all. Ah, truly — whose heart have you become so infatuated with, that you no longer even show affection toward me? Knowledgeable people give proof that you keep Vrishabhanu's daughter Radha as your beloved through this illicit bond, and that you gaze at her lovingly in secret. This matter of your loving bond with Radha was kept concealed by Shukdev and Naradji within the Bhagwat itself, and Parikshit, on hearing the Bhagwat, gained only a faint, partial sense of it. So your virtues and faults together cannot be told in full — yet Narsinh Mehta, composing this hymn, sings your praise; and it is for the sake of the wager of these Harmala hymns that Narsinh Mehta is moved to such passion — for who besides me, he says, will sing such praise of you?

A second hymn of the same sentiment appears in the Harmala as follows:

Raga Dev Gandhar (Ashavari) (Najar notebook no.28, p.420):

_Maahare mandalik su padi chhe hod re, mune tahara charan joyaana kod re, mune bhav bandhanthi chhod re, tamo jakh maarso mune haar aapo. Tek. Mune tamo vecho to vechau re, kaache taantne baandhi jaau re, hun gun govindnaa gaau re. ||1|| Tune gujar dhanai baandhati taani re, tyaare hun mukaavto saarangpaani re, men to pothamtaa tahaari jaani re. ||2|| Lok varvaan bole chhe maharaan re, dhaankya maharaan ke ughaadis taharaan re, taharaan manadaan haju nathi haaryaa re. ||3|| Tune vrikshabhaansuta rahi chhe raakhi re, te to mahara manmaan rahyo chhun saankhi re, men karnaa taraahi bhaakhi re. ||4|| Amo naagar batak bolaa kahaae, kahyaa kathan na raakhie hooiye re, taam vinaa sharan amo kone rahiye re. ||5|| Taharo narasaiyo rosh bharaay re, mujh vinaa jas taaraa kon gaay re, tun van vaahaare maharaari kon dhaay re. ||6||_ (I have made a wager with [King] Mandalik regarding you; my only longing is to behold your feet. Free me from the bondage of this worldly existence — though it may cost me, give me the wager. If you sell me, I will be sold; I will bind myself with a fragile thread, and still I will go on singing Govind's praises. Gujar Dhanai used to bind you up tightly, and I would free you, O Sarangpani; I have come to know your very helplessness. People speak ill of me — shield my faults, or I will expose yours; your heart has not yet softened. You keep Vrishabhanu's daughter as your beloved; this I bear silently within my own heart — this much mercy have I shown you. We Nagars speak plainly, and we do not withhold what is said or done — without you, in whose refuge should we remain? Your Narsinh Mehta grows angry — without me, who will sing your praise, and without me, who will run to my aid?)

Raghu Kahanji's mother, Baheniba, sang the hymn concerning Bhoja Gujar — "went to sell curd at Mathura" — thereby recalling this episode of Bhoja Gujar's life. Vaishnav Jivandasji then said: Bhojo, that is you, and Dhanbai, that is her. Vaishnavji then accepted this account. (Note — I, Jagdish, expressing my own view, say that since it was by the grace of Sadguru Jivandasji that I was given the strength and inspiration to write this account of the samagam, it seems to me that this Dhanbai is, at the present time, none other than Baheniba, Raghu Kahanji's mother, who sings Narsinh Mehta's hymn — the very same one who served Jivanji during the Krishna avatar is the same one who is serving Jivanji now. Ram-Kabir's Dhanbai has come here as Baheniba; my respectful [pranam] to them — Ramkabir.)

Vaishnav Jivandasji then asked Bhoja: will you take prasad? Bhoje said: Maharaj, whatever we take there [in that manner], that I will take — bring that [milk-food]. Then the lady brought gorasa [a milk-based offering]. The elder [Jivanji's son] Vasandas then rose to fetch a leaf-plate. Vaishnav Jivandasji asked: Bhoja, in what will you take your prasad? Bhoje answered: Maharaj, in whatever manner we receive it there, in that manner I will take it. So the elder Vasandas did not go to fetch a leaf-plate. That same day, at Vaishnav Jivandasji's temple, Harmabai gave Bhoja the curd-prasad, which Bhoja received by cupping both hands together. Then Bhojo said: now I am satisfied. After that he sought leave and made this plea: erase all my faults, whatever they may be. Vaishnav Jivandasji then said: Bhoja, your faults — whatever they were, from the past and up until this present day, have all been removed by the grace of Shri Kripanath. Having received that prasad, and having taken leave and blessing from Vaishnavji, Gujar Bhojo made his pranam to his own place. The very moment he made that pranam, Bhoja's release and deliverance took place, and he then reached Shri Kripanath. Thus was the episode of Bhoja Gujar completed. After this, the Vaishnav proceeded to reside at Dhanora.

Pu. Yadunath writes, in notebook 67, page 38: I heard the account of Bhojagujar from my mother, Gangaba, sitting in her lap. She would demonstrate the "cupped hands" gesture — interlocking the little finger of the right hand with the little finger of the left hand, forming a cup-like shape with the hands — and would say that this is how Bhoja drank the curd-prasad.

I, Jagdish, have likewise demonstrated to devotees and to Najar, with my own hands, what this cupped-hand gesture looks like. I have seen this with my own eyes, and I remember it.

Before Jivandasji Maharaj, Bhoja established proof of having been Krishna's companion during the Dvapar-age Krishna-lila, by reminding him of the episode of Brahmaji stealing the calves. That this same soul, who had once been Krishna's companion during Krishna's lila, should meet with Jivanji Maharaj, is a matter of pride for us; it is our great good fortune to meet one who had direct contact with Shri Krishna. Bhoja recalled the episode of Brahma and the calves of Krishna; Kabirji sang of this matter in a hymn in Raga Bhairav, as follows:

_Kaag kit hoi brijme aayo, avigatki gat aap bhulaayo._ (Becoming a crow and an insect, [Brahma] came into Braj — he himself forgot the true nature of the Imperishable [the Lord].)

Brahmaji took the form of a crow, and also the form of a fish, and tried in this way to obtain the Lord's prasad, yet the Lord never gave him the opportunity to receive it. Narsinh Mehta, too, has described this divine play:

Raga Gaud Malar Thal:

_Aa jone govalamaan game, govindaraay re dado re jame, jagan kare tahaan nikat na aave, jai aahiradamaan rame. ||1|| Aap aapnaan maathaan sahu laine, prabhujini aag daakhe re, shaak paak naahna vidh athaanaan, joi jaadav raache re. ||2|| Tyaare brahmajie man vichaaryun, meen tanun roop lije, jamunajimaan chalu lese, chaturbhuj mahaa prasaad paamije. ||3|| Antarjaamie tatkshan jaanyun, brahmaa meen tanun roop laavyo re, Narasaiyaacha swami chatur shiromani, kaamlie kar loharaavya. ||4||_ (See how much the Lord loves being with the cowherds — Govind eats their simple, humble fare there. Where a great sacrifice is performed, he will not even go near it, and yet he goes and plays among the lowly Ahir folk. Each one brings his own bundle of food and offers it before the Lord; seeing the vegetables, dishes, and various pickles, the Yadava [Krishna] rejoices. Then Brahmaji thought to himself: let me take the form of a fish, so that when the Lord comes to rinse His hands in the Yamuna, I, the four-armed one, shall receive that great prasad. But the all-knowing Lord instantly perceived that Brahma had come in the form of a fish; so Narsinh Mehta's Lord, foremost among the wise, had his hands wiped instead upon a blanket by the cowherds.)

Narsinh Mehta says: ah, look how much the Lord loves being with the cowherds; he eats the finest food together with them. Even if someone performs a great sacrifice (yajna), the Lord does not go near it, yet this same Lord goes and plays among the cowherd folk. Everyone brings his own bundle of food and offers it before the Lord; seeing the vegetables, dishes, and the various kinds of pickles, Shri Krishna becomes delighted. At that time Brahmaji thought to himself that he would take on the form of a fish, so that when the Lord came to wash his hands in the Yamuna, he could obtain that great prasad. But the Lord, who knows the innermost heart, instantly knew that Brahmaji had come in the form of a fish; therefore the Lord, most clever among the clever, had his hands wiped instead upon a blanket by the cowherds — and did not allow Brahma to obtain his prasad.

In discussing Bhoja Gujar, the Ram Sanehi sadhu wrote out Kabirji's Bijak hymn, Shabd 3, referring to the body and its senses as a household; this hymn was presented in Kabir Pani, year 1, issue 4, page 6, and its meaning was beautifully explained there. In it, the king of Riva is said to have counted, among those given over to durmati [perverse intellect], those who take the self [ego] to be the ultimate truth — reckoning among them the followers of "I am Brahman" as well as the atheists.

The spirit of Bhoja Gujar, which had attached itself to Rambai, wife of the goldsmith Keshavdas Zadeshwariya, was delivered by Jivanji Maharaj in Samvat 1716. That goldsmith became the devotee Uda, and established the Uda faith in Surat district. In the lineage of the mahants of the Surat seat, Naranadas is named as the first acharya of the Surat seat; this Naranadas is [also known as] Vasantdas, the eldest son of Jivandasji. Thus, through the propagation carried out by Naranadas as well as by the goldsmith Keshavdas, the Uda faith spread in Surat district. Not much particular information is available about Keshavdas; but when the devotee Narsinhbhai Ramji, of the Naaria Khadki quarter in Vadodara, was working in Vadsad, a goldsmith lived next to his residence. One evening, when Narsinh the devotee (bhagat) began to recite the evening arati, that goldsmith, on hearing the arati of Padmanabh, began to say: Bhagat, where did you get this arati of ours from?
